
-----------------

Introduction
============
We follow @ONeillRoberts-1999 in considering a data set obtained from a smallpox outbreak 
in a closed community of 120
individuals in Abakaliki, Nigeria [see @Bailey-1975, p. 125]. 
Removals are separated by the following 
interremoval times (measured in days, but with `0` adjusted to `ε > 0` in order to avoid coincidences).
Specific infectivity and removal rates are defined according to suggestions in @ONeillRoberts-1999
derived from a maximum likelihood analysis devised by Frank Ball.
```{julia}
#| label: initialization
population     = 120
ε              = 0.001 
interremovals  = [13, 7, 2, 3, ε, ε, 1, 4, 5, 3, 2, ε, 2, ε, 5, 3, 1, 4, ε, 1, 
                   1, 1, 2, ε, 1, 5, ε, 5, 5] 
α, β           = 0.0008, 0.088 
size           = length(interremovals) + 1 
cremoval_times = accumulate(+, interremovals) 
pushfirst!(cremoval_times, 0) 
duration = 10 + maximum(cremoval_times) ;
```
Note that the first `CRemoval` is deemed to have happened at time `0`.

We create maximal and minimal initial evolutions `evmin0` and `evmax0`, deriving from the most
minimal and maximal initial conditions possible,
under the reasonable assumption that all actual removals have been observed  as `CRemoval`s by time `{julia} duration`,
when our plots end,
(This considerably speeds up the simulation.)
```{julia}
#| label: setting up extremal evolutions
initial     = SIR(0, population - 1, 1, 0)
initial_min = SIR(0, population - 1, 1, 0)
initial_max = SIR(0, population - size, size, 0)

evmin0 = extremal_evolution(initial_min, duration, cremoval_times, 
    maximal=false) ;
evmax0 = extremal_evolution(initial_max, duration, cremoval_times, 
    maximal=true, all_cremovals_observed=true) ;
```
Plot `duration =` `{julia} duration` is set at `{julia} duration - maximum(cremoval_times)` days after the final removal,
a choice based on purely photogenic reasons.

The random `seed!` is fixed, in order to ensure repeatability.
```{julia}
#| label: initializing random seed
seed!(6) ;
```

===========================================

```{julia}
axes_plot = plot(uflow,

))

    style(line_width=theme.trail, default_color=theme.scaffold))) 

lines_plot = new_figure(axes_plot,
    Scale.y_continuous(labels=(initial.n ≤ EpidemicsUtilities.MAXPOP ?
        i -> EpidemicsUtilities.timelinelabels_circled(i; n=initial.n) :
        i -> EpidemicsUtilities.timelinelabels_bracketed(i; n=initial.n))),
    Guide.ylabel("Time lines")) ;
```



Implementation
==============
We have assumed the first observed removal to happen at time zero, and
we need further to assume a Bayesian prior distribution for the numbers of infectives at this time.
Under the assumption that all removals are observed, we know the size of the epidemic
must equal the number of `CRemoval`s plus the initial removal which triggered the data collection
exercise.

One possible prior distribution would be a uniform prior
over the range of possibilities which would not be able to lead to further removals being observed
after the completion of the observation period.
(This means that no removals can take place after the
last `CRemoval` (and therefore that no infectives can occur after the last `CRemoval`!).
This seems unduly pessimistic: it is possible to _compute_ a reasonable prior distribution
given α and β.
```{julia}
#| label: setup simulation
min_cremovals = [CRemoval(t, n) for (n, t) in enumerate(cremoval_times)]
iv_null  = CInnovation(initial.n, Infection[], Removal[], min_cremovals) 
```

The argument runs as follows. Assume that there is one index case and that all 
actual removals at _whatever_ time
are observed and are registered as `CRemoval`s. 
In that case one can argue that the relevant distribution 
(which is to say, pertaining to the _unconditioned_ epidemic!) for the
number of infectives at time `0` is the total number who have been infected up to the first actual
removal, less one (the removal!). Now before the initial observation
the relevant process undergoes a sequence of 
infection/removal transitions,
finishing when the first removal occurs. Rates after \(m\) infections (including the index infection),
in a population of size \(n\), are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{infection at rate }& (n-m) m \alpha \\
\text{removal at rate }  &  m \beta
\end{aligned}
\]
and so the chance that the next transition is an infection is 
\[
\frac{(n-m) m \alpha}{(n-m) m \alpha + m \beta}\quad=\quad
\frac{(n-m)\alpha }{(n-m)\alpha + \beta}
\quad=\quad
\frac{1}{1+ \frac{1}{n-m}\frac{\beta}{\alpha}}\,.
\]
In the particular case being considered, we are dealing with \(n=`{julia} population`\) 
and \(\alpha = `{julia} α`\), \(\beta = `{julia} β`\), so
the chance of the next transition being an infection is (for the first transition)
\[
\frac{1}{1+ \frac{1}{n-1}\frac{\beta}{\alpha}}\quad=\quad
`{julia} 1/(1+ β/((population-1)α))`
\]
and then monotonically decays for further transitions up to the point of the first removal. 
So one can argue that the number of `Infection`s at time `0` is sub-Geometric
(version with smallest value equal to `1`, since we require at least one `Infection` at time zero!)
with this success parameter.

This needs a little more Bayesian justification, based on some prior for the (negative) time 
at which the index case is infected, but we omit this for now.


We introduce the notion of an `AbstractInnovationStart` 
(eventually to be hidden in `EpidemicsCFTP`:
```{julia}
#| label: Defining `InnovationStart`s
import Random: rand, AbstractRNG, GLOBAL_RNG

"""
    AbstractInnovationStart

This abstract type holds information which can be generated by `rand`, and
then in turn can be combined with a `CEvolution` using `⋄` to generate
a proposal of a new `initial` state whose acceptance depends on whether
the `CEvolution` meets required conditions when started with the proposal.
"""
abstract type AbstractInnovationStart end

"""
    InnovationStart_IS{Categorical{Real, Vector{Real}}} <: AbstractInnovationStart
    
The `AbstractInnovationStart` information is simply a specific `Categorical` distribution
to be used to propose a `SIR` for the new initial state. Combined with the `CEvolution`
test this carries out the equivalent of an independence sampler move (the suffix `_IS`
refers to Independence Sampler!).
### Example
jldoctest
prob  = Real[0.8, 0.2]
prior = Categorical(prob)
InnovationStart_IS(prior)

# output

InnovationStart_IS(Categorical{Real, Vector{Real}}(support=Base.OneTo(2), p=Real[0.8, 0.2]))

"""
struct InnovationStart_IS <: AbstractInnovationStart
    prior::Categorical

function InnovationStart_IS(prior::Categorical)
   return new(prior)
end    

@doc """
    InnovationStart_IS(Vector{Real})

Shortcut to constructing an `InnovationStart_IS`: simply supply the vector of probabilities
to be used to define the required `Categorical` distribution.
### Example
jldoctest
prob=Real[0.7, 0.3]
InnovationStart_IS(prob)

# output

InnovationStart_IS(Categorical{Real, Vector{Real}}(support=Base.OneTo(2), p=Real[0.7, 0.3]))

"""
function InnovationStart_IS(prob::Vector{S}) where S<: Real
   prior = Categorical(prob)
   return new(prior)
end
end
```

Here is the code for sampling from an `InnovationStart_IS`. ***This will need improving!***
```{julia}
#| label: Random samplers
function rand(rng::AbstractRNG, iv_ST::InnovationStart_IS)
    return rand(rng, iv_ST.prior)
end
 
  
function rand(iv_ST::InnovationStart_IS)
    return rand(GLOBAL_RNG, iv_ST)
end
```

We define a vector of probabilities given as products of transition probabilities as 
in the above theoretical description. Notice that here we are implicitly using
the epidemic size threshold induced by requiring that the initial number of infectives
must be less than the number of `CRemoval`s.
```{julia}
#| label: prior distribution 
function transition_probability(k)
    return ((population - k) * α) / ((population - k) * α + β)
end
survival = [transition_probability(k) for k in 1:length(min_cremovals)]
priorprob = (1 .- survival) .* pushfirst!(accumulate(*, survival[1:(end-1)]), 1)
push!(priorprob, 1 - sum(priorprob))
iv_ST = InnovationStart_IS(priorprob)

prior_df = DataFrame(k=1:(1+size), probability=priorprob)
plt = plot(prior_df, x=:k, y=:probability,
    Guide.xlabel("Number of initial infectives", orientation=:horizontal),
    Guide.ylabel("Prior probability", orientation=:vertical),
    Geom.bar)
draw(PDF("image/prior.pdf"), plt)
print((1+size))
```


![Probability mass function for prior for number of initial infectives.](image/prior.pdf)

We'll need a stream of tuples of `Innovation`s and proposals to change `initial` conditions.
The function `innovation_stream` supplies a single stream of tuples each giving
an `Innovation` and a proposal to change initial condition.
For now we simply ensure this is long enough to fuel the entire CFTP process,
though in principle it would be easy to extend this as required!
Note that `generate_innovation` uses the `size` keyword parameter to exclude
`Infection`s which if activated would cause epidemic size to rise above the
specified `size`.
```{julia}
#| label: function `innovation_stream`
import EpidemicsCFTP: proposed_sir
function innovation_stream(cycle_length;
            evmin=evmin0, iv_null=iv_null, duration=duration, α=α, β=β, size=size)
    stream, initial = [], evmin0.initial
    for iteration ∈ 1:cycle_length
        # `Innovation`
        iv = generate_innovation(iv_null, duration; α=α, β=β, size=size)
        # Proposed initial infection levels: distribution `prior` constructed above.
        proposed_i = rand(iv_ST)
        push!(stream, (iv, proposed_sir(initial, proposed_i)))
    end
    return stream
end ;
```

Our update proposes a change in the initial condition
for a `CEvolution`, which will be accepted only if it leads to a valid `CEvolution`.
At present this corresponds to an independence sampler move
though it should be possible to vary this to be a simple Random Walk Metropolis
sampler (_simple RWM_).
In general, care needs to be taken that monotonicity is maintained!
[A similar situation concerning spatial point processes is discussed in @KendallMoeller-2000.]

Using this, 
a function `single_frame` updates minimal and maximal `CEvolution`s by a single algorithmic step.
Note that we vary the initial number of infectives using a separate accept/reject step
in the update. Note that `proposed_sir` here simply supplies a proposed initial number
of `Infection`s; other aspects do not affect the result.
```{julia}
#| label: function `single_frame`
function single_frame(work, evmin, evmax, iv, proposed_sir; duration=duration, theme=theme)
    evmin = evmin ⋄ iv ▷ proposed_sir 
    evmax = evmax ⋄ iv ▷ proposed_sir 

    # Omit next conditional statement once thoroughly tested!
    if !(evmin ⪯ evmax)
        error("Monotonicity fails")
    end

    if evmin ≃ evmax
        draw_evolution!(work, evmin, duration, theme=theme, 
                    select=BOUNDARIES, specified_color=coalesce_colour, specified_opacity=1.0)
    else
        draw_evolution!(work, evmin, duration, theme=theme, 
                    #select=BOUNDARIES, specified_color=min_spectrum[1])
                    select=BOUNDARIES, specified_color=min_spectrum[1], specified_opacity=0.2)
        draw_evolution!(work, evmax, duration, theme=theme,
                    #select=BOUNDARIES, specified_color=max_spectrum[1])
                    select=BOUNDARIES, specified_color=max_spectrum[1], specified_opacity=0.2)
    end

    return evmin, evmax
end ;
```

Most of the work of the CFTP algorithm will be done by the `cycle` function.
Note that previous cycles are included in the plots as relevant. Ideally we should plot
these as greyed out, but this is a matter for later.
```{julia}
#| label: function `cycle`
function cycle(stream, canvas; 
        evmin0=evmin0, evmax0=evmax0, tag="demo-e", lines_plot=lines_plot, theme=theme)
    work = deepcopy(lines_plot)
    evmin = deepcopy(evmin0)
    evmax = deepcopy(evmax0)
    iteration = 0
    legend  = lpad(iteration, 4, "0")
    if iteration < length(stream)
        legend2 = "-$(lpad(length(stream)-iteration, 4, "0")):"
    else
        legend2 = "$(lpad(length(stream)-iteration, 4, "0")): "
    end
    draw_evolution!(work, evmin, duration, theme=theme,
                    select=BOUNDARIES, specified_color=min_spectrum[1])
    draw_evolution!(work, evmax, duration, theme=theme,
                    select=BOUNDARIES, specified_color=max_spectrum[1])
    logo  = "Minimum and maximum evolutions at algorithmic time step"
    title = "$logo $legend2"
    about = "Cycle at time $legend2 begun at $(-length(stream))"
    info  = Guide.annotation(compose(context(), font("Helvetica"), fontsize(12pt), 
                    text(0.4w, 0.95h, about), fill("tomato")))
    image = new_figure(work, info; title=title)
    draw(PNG("animation/$tag-$legend.png"), image)
    draw(PDF("animation/$tag-$legend.pdf"), image)
    
    lstream = "-$(lpad(length(stream), 4, "0"))"
    
    for (iteration, pair) ∈ enumerate(stream)
        (evmin, evmax) = single_frame(canvas[iteration], evmin, evmax, pair...)

        legend = lpad(iteration, 4, "0")
        legend2 = "-$(lpad(length(stream)-iteration, 4, "0")):"

        about1 = "Cycle at time $legend2"
        about2 = "begun at $lstream"
        info  = Guide.annotation(compose(context(), font("Helvetica"), fontsize(12pt), 
                        text(0.4w, 0.95h, about1), text(0.7w, 0.95h, about2), fill("tomato")))

        if (evmin ≃ evmax)
            title  = "$logo $legend2 [COALESCED]"
            signal = Guide.annotation(compose(context(), font("Helvetica-Bold"), fontsize(14pt), 
                        text(0.4w, 0.8h, "COALESCED"), fill("tomato")))
            image  = new_figure(canvas[iteration], info, signal; title=title)
        else
            title  = "$logo $legend2"
            image  = new_figure(canvas[iteration], info; title=title)
        end
        draw(PNG("animation/$tag-$legend.png"), image)
        if mod(iteration, 10) == 0
            draw(PDF("animation/$tag-$legend.pdf"), image)
        end
    end
    draw(PNG("animation/$tag.png"), image)
    draw(PDF("animation/$tag.pdf"), image)
end ;
```

This code is used to plot an entire CFTP sequence of sequences of updates in algorithmic time: see [Appendix @sec-figures].
I suspect that considerable speed-up could be achieved by _not_ plotting each frame of each cycle!

Graphical illustration of CFTP {#sec-figures}
==============================

In this appendix we display an entire evolution of a CFTP run, always starting with minimal and maximal evolutions
`evmin0` and `evmax0` given above. 
An [animated `GIF`](file:///home/wilfrid/ms/PerfectEpidemics/julia/animation-demo.gif) displays the entire CFTP,
evolving in logical time and re-starting earlier and earlier till coalescence is achieved!

The work of each CFTP cycle is carried out by the function `cycle`. Note that we have not yet automated 
how CFTP works through cycles.
```{julia}
#| label: building figures
max_length = 256
stream = innovation_stream(max_length)
canvas = [deepcopy(lines_plot) for iteration ∈ 1:max_length]

for (epithet, cycle_length) ∈ [("a", 8), ("b", 16), ("c", 32), ("d", 64), ("e", 128)] 
    cycle(stream[max_length - cycle_length + 1:max_length], 
        canvas[max_length - cycle_length + 1:max_length], 
        tag="demo-$epithet")
end
```

Now we create a `GIF` of the entire CFTP run, working with `ImageMagick` on the command-line.
(Construction might be quicker if run in memory!)
```{julia}
#| label: creating GIF using CLI
lexicon = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"] 
dt1 = 15
dt2 = 300
for epithet ∈ lexicon
    prefix = "animation/demo-$epithet"
    run(`convert -delay $dt1 $prefix-\*.png -delay $dt2 $prefix.png -layers Optimize $prefix.gif`)
end
run(`convert -loop 1 animation/demo-\*.gif -layers Optimize animation-demo.gif`)
run(`rm $(["animation/demo-$epithet.gif" for epithet in lexicon])`) ;
```

Final (coalescent) cycle
------------------------
There follow a selection of figures illustrating the final cycle of the CFTP algorithm, 
sampled at every ten steps from step `10` onwards up to step `250` and also displaying runs of previous cycles
where appropriate.
We start with the initial configuration of maximal and minimal evolutions at time `0`,
and then plot continuation of the final CFTP cycle. Note that times are displayed
as _negative_, counting up to time `0`!

It would also be better to display previous cycles as greyed out. Note however that
